These benefits include: improved freshwater quality (as a result of stopping  conversion of native forest to plantations, which have a pronounced negative  impact on freshwater), and employment opportunities. The Reserve has hired 6  community members full-time as rangers and in their maintenance department;  5 people are hired seasonally as firefighters; and a native forest restoration  project directly contracts 8 other community members.  Other services involve  more sporadic employment such as the development of trails, fence building,  construction or the production of specific products.  Ecotourism has provided an  indirect form of employment for community members with 14 local guides and a  variety of local businesses related to tourism, lodging and restaurants. A chart  detailing various development initiatives that have contributed to increased well  being, is included as an appendix. Furthermore, TNC employs a Social  Programs Coordinator who is present on site to develop community programs.   Clearly this level of connection and support provides a net benefit for the  communities, in that it was not part of the baseline scenario.  In part this is due  to the fact that forestry companies typically do not have explicit social objectives  or personnel dedicated to developing social programs.
